categories.label: Knowledge and Research Gaps on Standard Contract Suitability for MMC
categories.memo: Captures the identified absence or scarcity of research and standard-form guidance specifically addressing MMC/MOC/MiC contractual relationships, risk allocation, and delivery method selection.

codes.label: Absence of MiC/MOC-specific contractual research
codes.description: Literature lacks studies on contractual relationships, dispute cases, and risk allocation specific to modular/off-site construction, despite maturity of general MMC risk research.

codes.label: Untested suitability of risk-sharing standard forms
codes.description: Standard forms built on risk-sharing principles (FIDIC, NEC) have not been evaluated for their fitness in MiC/MMC project contexts.

codes.label: Undetermined best delivery method for early contractor/supplier involvement
codes.description: No consensus exists on which project delivery method (DB, IPD, EPC, BOT) best supports the early contractor/supplier involvement and design liability sharing that MMC requires.

codes.label: No standard contracts exist for MOC in Canada
codes.description: Canadian MOC projects have no dedicated standard contract and instead adapt conventional on-site contracts, which increases dispute potential and was confirmed by absence of standard-form use in MOC litigation.

categories.label: Contract Clarity, Drafting Quality and Readability
categories.memo: Addresses linguistic, structural and interpretive qualities of contract text (jargon, ambiguity, modifications) that affect how well standard forms function, independent of MMC content per se but foundational to adapting them.

codes.label: Ambiguity and vague terminology
codes.description: Vague or undefined terms in contract clauses create differing interpretations and are a primary cause of conflicts and claims.

codes.label: Legal jargon and readability barriers
codes.description: Excessive legal terminology, drafted by lawyers but used by engineers, reduces contract comprehensibility and increases dispute risk.

codes.label: Effects of modifying standard forms on clarity
codes.description: Client-driven modifications to standard forms (FIDIC, NEC, JCT) to meet project needs often reduce readability and can introduce new ambiguity despite the original clarity benefits of standard text.

codes.label: Structural and stylistic drafting factors
codes.description: Scope complexity, incoherence between clauses, negative language style, and lack of visual representation (diagrams/charts) independently affect contract transparency and trust.

codes.label: Root-cause vs symptom approach to drafting fixes
codes.description: Effective contract clarification should target underlying grammar/terminology/format issues rather than superficial fixes like shortening sentences.

categories.label: Analysis of Particular/General Conditions and Obligation Extraction
categories.memo: Focuses on empirical/text-analytic methods for examining how general and particular conditions distribute obligations and risk, and what this implies for adapting contracts to MMC.

codes.label: Function of particular conditions in modifying general conditions
codes.description: Particular conditions typically clarify obligations and definitions rather than fundamentally altering the risk-mitigation function of general conditions; task-change/variation procedures remain largely fixed.

sub_codes.label: Interpretation clauses as primary site of modification
sub_codes.description: Definitional/interpretive clauses are the most heavily modified subfunction, tailoring general terms to project specifics.

sub_codes.label: Task Changes procedures remain rigid
sub_codes.description: Variation and value engineering procedures are essentially unmodified across particular conditions, indicating industry-wide rigidity in change management clauses.

sub_codes.label: Adaptation provisions least modified
sub_codes.description: Clauses addressing future uncertainty are rarely changed because contingencies are difficult to foresee even at drafting.

codes.label: Obligation extraction and quantitative risk balance assessment
codes.description: Systematic extraction of obligations/clauses from contracts can reveal numerical imbalances in risk allocation between parties, useful for pre-contract risk assessment.

codes.label: Clause hierarchy: conditions, warranties, innominate terms
codes.description: Not all contract clauses carry equal weight; distinguishing essential conditions from minor warranties helps prioritize risk-sensitive drafting.

categories.label: Variation and Change Management Clauses
categories.memo: Covers how standard contracts define, value, limit, and process changes in scope, and the specific complications these provisions pose for off-site fabrication where late changes are costly.

codes.label: Valuation methods for variations
codes.description: Clearly defined valuation methods for variations are critical to fair cost compensation and dispute minimization.

codes.label: Change-in-law and unforeseen condition clauses
codes.description: Absence of change-in-law clauses forces reliance on claims rather than smoother variation procedures; explicit change order/compensation mechanisms are needed to manage unforeseen conditions.

codes.label: Value engineering benefit-sharing terms
codes.description: Value engineering clauses only benefit contractors when profit-sharing terms are balanced; unilateral employer-favoring terms discourage participation.

codes.label: Limitation and right-to-decline variation clauses
codes.description: Clear limits on variation scope and contractor rights to decline out-of-scope variations protect contractors from unbounded risk, particularly relevant where late changes disrupt fabrication.

codes.label: Terminology differences across standard forms for variations
codes.description: FIDIC, AIA, and NEC use different terminology and procedural philosophies for handling variations, reflecting differing traditions relevant to MMC-specific scope changes.

codes.label: Difficulty and cost of late scope changes in off-site fabrication
codes.description: Because off-site construction requires finalized scope/design before manufacturing begins, later changes are disproportionately disruptive and costly compared to on-site construction.

categories.label: Payment, Advance Financing and Progress Claim Mechanisms
categories.memo: Addresses how standard contract payment clauses are structured around on-site progress and are misaligned with off-site manufacturing's upfront financing needs.

codes.label: Progress payment clauses tied to site delivery
codes.description: Standard clauses (e.g., CCDC 14 5.2.3) only permit payment claims when work is performed and products delivered to site, disadvantaging MOC contractors whose work occurs off-site.

codes.label: Ambiguous definition of 'Products' for off-site claims
codes.description: Provisions allowing claims for delivered-but-not-incorporated products (e.g., CCDC 5.2.8) are ambiguous as to whether prefabricated modules qualify as 'Products'.

codes.label: Need for upfront/advance payment provisions
codes.description: MMC/off-site work requires significant upfront financing for factory production, materials, and specialized equipment, which standard contracts' progress-based payment structures do not accommodate.

codes.label: Unclear payment terms as leading litigation cause in MOC
codes.description: Unclear payment terms are identified as the predominant cause of litigation specifically in modular/off-site construction court cases, contrasted with change-related disputes in conventional construction.

codes.label: Payment delay effects on manufacturer cash flow
codes.description: Owner payment delays disrupt manufacturer/supplier cash flow disproportionately in off-site construction due to upfront cost commitments, potentially triggering contractual penalties.

categories.label: Risk Allocation, Insurance and Liability Provisions
categories.memo: Concerns how contracts assign risk, insurance responsibility, and liability among parties, and gaps specific to transportation, care of works, and design liability in MMC.

codes.label: Care of works and transportation insurance gaps
codes.description: No clear contractual treatment exists for contractor responsibility and insurance coverage during module transportation, a distinct MMC risk not addressed by conventional contract wording.

codes.label: General risk allocation principles and imbalance
codes.description: Risk should be allocated to the party best able to manage it; unmanaged or unbalanced risk-sharing increases costs and disputes, and standard forms are often skewed toward client interests.

codes.label: Liability and indemnification clarity for prefabricated components
codes.description: Contracts often lack clarity on guarantees, liabilities, and indemnification specific to prefabricated/modular components.

codes.label: Design liability sharing with manufacturers/suppliers
codes.description: MMC requires shifting some design/engineering liability to manufacturers, a reallocation not well reflected in standard contract risk provisions.

codes.label: Insurance mechanism differences across collaborative contract forms
codes.description: Standard collaborative forms (ConsensusDocs 300, AIA C-191) differ in mandatory insurance consultants, coverage duration, and requirements, creating ambiguity if unspecified.

categories.label: Dispute Resolution, Suspension and Termination Provisions
categories.memo: Covers contractual mechanisms for handling disputes, work suspension, and termination, and their particular relevance to fabrication-dependent projects.

codes.label: Absent MMC-specific dispute resolution research
codes.description: Despite likely disputes in real MiC/MOC projects, standard forms and literature lack guidance on dispute resolution processes tailored to modular/off-site construction.

codes.label: Suspension and termination ambiguity
codes.description: Ambiguous rights and obligations regarding suspension/termination, including asymmetric owner termination discretion, are recurring sources of dispute in collaborative and traditional contracts.

codes.label: Tiered dispute resolution procedures
codes.description: Structured, escalating dispute resolution procedures (mediation before binding methods) are recommended to reduce cost and disruption of disputes.

codes.label: Illegal/improper work suspension in off-site contexts
codes.description: Improper suspension is a major dispute cause in off-site construction because it disrupts pre-arranged fabrication schedules and procurement, more so than in conventional on-site work.

categories.label: Collaborative and Integrated Delivery Contract Frameworks
categories.memo: Examines multiparty, relational contract models (IPD, ConsensusDocs, AIA C-191, CCDC30) as alternatives better suited to MMC's need for early involvement, shared risk, and cross-stakeholder integration.

codes.label: Multiparty agreements and shared risk/reward as IPD-defining features
codes.description: IPD is characterized by multiparty agreements, shared risk/reward, and early involvement, differentiating it from traditional risk-allocating contracts.

codes.label: Incentive and compensation alignment mechanisms
codes.description: Cost-saving incentive structures in collaborative contracts aim to align behavior, but parties unfamiliar with these mechanisms may fail to implement them properly.

codes.label: Data sharing and BIM protocols in contracts
codes.description: Collaborative contract forms require explicit provisions establishing technology/software platforms and data-sharing standards to support integrated MMC information exchange.

codes.label: IPD/DfMA synergy and need for dedicated guidelines
codes.description: DfMA implementation benefits from IPD-type contractual frameworks addressing people integration, but dedicated guidance linking IPD contract forms (e.g., CCDC30) with DfMA is underdeveloped.

codes.label: Checklist tools for negotiating collaborative contract terms
codes.description: Structured checklists of contractual questions help unfamiliar parties negotiate clearer terms in collaborative delivery models, reducing ambiguity-driven disputes.

codes.label: Fragmentation barriers of traditional delivery contracts
codes.description: Traditional design-bid-build contracts create vertical, horizontal, and longitudinal fragmentation between stakeholders that hinders DfMA/MMC collaboration and knowledge retention across projects.

categories.label: Scope, Roles and Specification Definition for MMC/DfMA
categories.memo: Addresses how contracts define scope of work, stakeholder roles, and technical specifications relevant to prefabrication, and gaps causing confusion or duplication.

codes.label: Unclear scope of work and role definitions
codes.description: Lack of clearly defined scope of work and stakeholder roles/responsibilities in contracts leads to confusion, duplication, and complex negotiations in DfMA projects.

codes.label: Insufficient MOC-specific specifications
codes.description: Conventional contract specifications are inadequate and lack separate provisions for modular/off-site construction, contributing to missing-information disputes.

codes.label: Manufacturer flexibility and multiple sourcing clauses
codes.description: Contracts often lack references to multiple manufacturers, limiting sourcing flexibility needed for DfMA/MMC supply chains.

codes.label: Design constraints from transportation/shipment method
codes.description: Module design is constrained by transportation and shipment choices, creating a distinct contractual/design ambiguity category not present in conventional construction.

categories.label: External and Jurisdictional Factors Affecting Contract Suitability
categories.memo: Covers logistics, regulatory, and industry-maturity factors external to the contract text itself but which contracts must account for to be suitable for MMC.

codes.label: Transportation and cross-jurisdictional regulation gaps
codes.description: Volumetric transportation difficulties and contradictory transportation regulations across jurisdictions are significant unaddressed sources of contractual ambiguity in modular construction.

codes.label: Local industry maturity and readiness
codes.description: Level of local industry adoption of modern construction practices affects project progress and should be considered in contract drafting, though this factor is underrepresented in actual litigation.

codes.label: Gap between literature-identified risks and actual litigation evidence
codes.description: Several MMC/MOC-specific risk factors emphasized in literature (transportation limits, industry readiness) do not appear in actual court case data, indicating disconnect between theorized and litigated contractual issues.

codes.label: Procurement strategy correlation with contractual ambiguity
codes.description: Sources of contractual ambiguity are strongly linked to the chosen procurement/delivery method, an area not fully explored due to limited case data on contract type.

categories.label: Procurement Routes and Policy Enablers for MMC-Suitable Contracts
categories.memo: Considers which procurement/delivery routes and policy conditions best support MMC contract suitability, including barriers from client behavior and public procurement practice.

codes.label: Design and Build as preferred but contested procurement route
codes.description: Design and Build fosters early supply chain involvement and single-point responsibility for MMC, though some argue it limits early engagement compared to models like IPI.

codes.label: Collaborative procurement mechanisms and public sector barriers
codes.description: Two-stage tendering and collaborative frameworks (e.g., FAC-1) are seen as necessary for MMC success, but public sector clients often fail to engage collaboratively or favor larger providers, disadvantaging smaller MMC firms.

codes.label: Policy and legislative reform as enabler
codes.description: Legislative and procurement policy reform is viewed as critical to removing structural barriers to MMC adoption in standard contracting practice.

codes.label: Client-imposed bespoke terms vs standard form preference
codes.description: MMC suppliers generally prefer standard forms (e.g., JCT) for simplicity, but clients often impose bespoke amendments to transfer risk, reflecting a tension in contract selection.

categories.label: Applicability of Specific CCDC Provisions to Off-Site/Modular Construction
categories.memo: Directly examines named CCDC clauses and forms in relation to MOC, forming the most direct evidence for the study's central research question.

codes.label: CCDC 14 suitability as design-build MOC form
codes.description: CCDC 14 is considered the most suitable existing standard form for MOC projects, though its native payment clause structure still assumes on-site delivery of work.

codes.label: CCDC 2 as dominant but non-MOC-specific form
codes.description: CCDC 2 stipulated price contract is the most commonly used standard contract in Canada but is not tailored to off-site/modular construction needs.

codes.label: Need for CCDC term modification to recognize modules as claimable products
codes.description: CCDC terminology (e.g., 'Products') needs explicit modification to clarify that fabricated modules qualify for partial payment claims before site delivery, and to extend insurance coverage during transport/storage.

codes.label: Lack of DfMA-compatible CCDC platforms
codes.description: Existing CCDC contract forms are not well aligned with DfMA platforms and processes, limiting their applicability to prefabrication-based delivery.
